source.title: Nonasymptotic theory for two-layer neural networks: Beyond the bias-variance trade-off

record.file_problem: None noted; the paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study theoretically derives generalization-risk bounds for regularized two-layer ReLU networks and argues that they imply double descent. This is a different approach from empirical sweeps of test error.
record.gate_note: The results are theoretical risk bounds and an illustrative plot of a bound, not measurements on trained networks. The paper also mentions double-descent results from prior work; those cited findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A theoretical (non-empirical) analysis. Its nonasymptotic prediction-error upper bounds for scaled-variation-regularized two-layer ReLU networks, over all widths m, trace a width-wise double-descent curve. It also makes an explicit argument against the claim that optimal regularization removes double descent (V6). This is a different method aimed at the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that nonasymptotic prediction bounds for scaled-variation-regularized two-layer ReLU networks reproduce double descent. Approximation error falls with width, while estimation error rises until about sqrt(n/(d log n)) and then saturates. The overparametrized valley is nearly minimax optimal over G and is lower than the first valley when the signal is strong. They argue that double descent is intrinsic and not removed by optimal regularization, and that random-feature models are suboptimal.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theoretical analysis of regularized two-layer ReLU networks and prediction-risk bounds, rather than an empirical model-size, epoch, or sample-size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The derived bounds use different regularization choices in the underparametrized and overparametrized regimes; the plotted example fixes d = 6, n = 1000, and ∥f*∥S²/σε² = 1.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimally tuned random-feature ridge estimators have a worst-case risk lower bound of order M/(d·min(m,n)^{1/d}) over GM, i.e. the curse of dimensionality.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-feature models are minimax-suboptimal relative to fully trained two-layer networks over variation-norm function classes.

record.problems: The evidence for double descent is theoretical: the main result is a prediction-error upper bound, and Figure 1 is an illustration based on that bound rather than an empirical sweep. The paper does not connect the bound's width-wise peak to the width at which training data are just fit.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant findings were left out. Theorems 2 and 6 concern empirical-risk/minimax bounds rather than a separate reported double-descent result; cited results from other work were excluded.

untested.parts: No empirical test-error sweep. Actual risk (rather than an upper bound) is not shown to rise. The peak is not tied to the interpolation threshold, and the analysis is limited to two-layer networks with explicit regularization.
Cross-model-class generality; only two-layer ReLU networks are analysed.
Discusses effective dimension (number of nonparallel directions) but does not test a single measure predicting peak location across axes.
No label-noise sweep, no multiple peaks, and no λ sweep on actual risk. Only the bound under rate-optimal λ is given.
It argues that width is the wrong complexity measure in the overparametrized regime, but never replots risk against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Condition (16): the second (overparametrized) valley is lower than the first only when the signal-to-noise ratio is large (roughly SNR > 1/3 when d ≫ log n). This shows the depth and benefit of the second descent depend on the noise level.
The double-descent bound persists with fixed d, so the phenomenon in this framework is not tied to high dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: All evidence is from upper bounds with unspecified constants, so the 'peak' is a feature of the bound and not a demonstrated rise in actual risk. The 'optimal' regularization is rate-optimal per regime, chosen for the proof, not tuned empirically. This weakens the V6 challenge. The reader's V6 'challenges' label is kept but qualified.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not empirically sweep model size or establish that the risk peak coincides with the size at which training data are just fit.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No study of test error as sample size increases near an interpolation threshold.
The paper analyzes two-layer ReLU networks and gives a random-feature lower bound, but does not test a general double-descent curve across model classes.
The paper discusses width-related effective dimension, but does not test whether one measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
The paper argues that double descent persists under its selected regularization, but does not sweep label-noise levels, test multiple peaks, or vary regularization to map peak dependence.
The paper does not replot or measure the second descent against an effective parameter count to test whether it becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: regularized two-layer ReLU network estimator g(·; θ̂)
rows.operation_detail: Combines the underparametrized and overparametrized theoretical bounds across width.

conditions.value: λ = min(λ1, λ2), with λ1 and λ2 defined in Theorems 3 and 4

rows.measure: Prediction-error upper bound and its implied width-wise shape
rows.value: C∥f*∥S² m−(d+3)/d + (σε² + ∥f*∥S²) min{√(d log n/n), md log n/n}; the authors state that this gives rise to a double-descent risk curve.
rows.uncertainty: With probability at least 1 − O(n−C1); constants C and C1 are not specified numerically.
rows.locator: Theorem 5 and discussion immediately following it
rows.note: The result is an upper-bound curve for a regularized estimator, not an empirical test-error sweep. The paper says its theory uses optimal choices of the regularization parameter and that double descent cannot be eliminated by such choices.
rows.check: For V1 the bound has a double-descent shape, but the bound peak sits near m1 ≍ sqrt(n/(d log n)), far below the interpolation width. The estimator is regularized, not interpolating. For V6 the state should read as the version failing: the authors say double descent is not removed by 'optimal' λ. That λ is rate-optimal for the bound (λ = min(λ1, λ2)), not tuned on actual risk, so for V6 the effect described (disappearance) is absent.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V1 and V6. Theorem 5 combines prediction-error upper bounds using λ=min(λ1,λ2). It establishes neither an actual-risk peak near first interpolation nor persistence of that peak under actual-risk-optimal regularization.
source_check.locator_found: Theorem 5 and following discussion, lines 972–1034; Section 6, lines 1170–1177.
source_check.problem: Observed overstates what an upper bound and its prescribed regularization schedule demonstrate.

relationships.condition: Theoretical width-wise upper bound for regularized two-layer ReLU networks, fixed d
relationships.reason: The combined bound falls to a valley at m0, rises to m1, then decreases to a flat second valley. The authors state that this reproduces double descent (r1–r4).
